name: Population
definition_quote: A population consists of the entire set of individuals or objects that you want to learn about.
plain_en: every individual or object of interest

name: Sample
definition_quote: A sample is a subset of the population that is selected for study.
plain_en: the part of a population studied

name: Statistics
definition_quote: The field of statistics is all about collecting, describing, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data.
plain_en: science of collecting and analyzing data

name: Parameter
definition_quote: A parameter is a numerical summary of a population, while a statistic is a numerical summary of sample data.
plain_en: numerical summary of a whole population

name: Statistic
definition_quote: A parameter is a numerical summary of a population, while a statistic is a numerical summary of sample data.
plain_en: numerical summary calculated from sample data

name: Conclusion in context
definition_quote: Conclusions should be given in context, that is, should refer back to the population in a real-world frame of reference.
plain_en: answer stated in the real-world setting

name: Data
definition_quote: Data are pieces of information about observational units (items or individuals).
plain_en: information recorded about individuals or objects

name: Observational unit
definition_quote: Data are pieces of information about observational units (items or individuals).
plain_en: item or individual being studied

name: Variables
definition_quote: Variables are characteristics that may change from one observational unit to another.
plain_en: characteristics that can vary between units

name: Categorical variable
definition_quote: A categorical variable (or qualitative variable) places individuals into groups called categories.
plain_en: variable placing individuals into groups

name: Qualitative variable
definition_quote: A categorical variable (or qualitative variable) places individuals into groups called categories.
plain_en: variable describing a category or group

name: Quantitative variable
definition_quote: A quantitative variable (or numerical variable) takes on values for a measurable quantity.
plain_en: variable measuring a numerical quantity

name: Frequency table
definition_quote: The values taken on by categorical variables can be organized into frequency tables or relative frequency tables.
plain_en: table counting values in each category

name: Relative frequency table
definition_quote: The values taken on by categorical variables can be organized into frequency tables or relative frequency tables.
plain_en: table showing proportions in each category

name: Frequency
definition_quote: Frequency gives the number of cases falling into each category, while relative frequency gives the proportion or percent of cases falling into each category.
plain_en: number of cases in a category

name: Relative frequency
definition_quote: Frequency gives the number of cases falling into each category, while relative frequency gives the proportion or percent of cases falling into each category.
plain_en: proportion of cases in a category

name: Distribution
definition_quote: The distribution of a variable describes the possible values the variable could assume and how often each of those values occurs.
plain_en: possible values and how often they occur

name: Bar chart
definition_quote: They can be represented graphically by displays such as bar charts (bar graphs) and pie charts.
plain_en: graph with bars for categories

name: Pie chart
definition_quote: They can be represented graphically by displays such as bar charts (bar graphs) and pie charts.
plain_en: circle divided into category slices

name: Discrete quantitative variable
definition_quote: A discrete quantitative variable takes on a finite or countable number of values.
plain_en: countable numerical variable with gaps

name: Continuous quantitative variable
definition_quote: A continuous quantitative variable can take on uncountable or infinite values with no gaps, such as heights and weights of students.
plain_en: numerical variable taking any value in an interval

name: Histogram
definition_quote: Histograms, which are useful for large data sets involving quantitative variables, show frequencies or relative frequencies with bars over intervals called bins.
plain_en: bars showing frequencies over intervals

name: Bin
definition_quote: Histograms, which are useful for large data sets involving quantitative variables, show frequencies or relative frequencies with bars over intervals called bins.
plain_en: interval used for histogram bars

name: Dotplot
definition_quote: A quantitative variable takes on numerical values for a measured or counted quantity. The values can be organized into frequency tables or relative frequency tables or can be represented graphically by displays such as dotplots, histograms, stemplots, cumulative relative frequency plots, or boxplots.
plain_en: graph with dots for each value

name: Stemplot
definition_quote: An alternative pictorial display, called a stemplot (also called a stem and leaf display), retains this individual information and is useful for giving a quick overview of a distribution, displaying the relative density and shape of the data.
plain_en: display splitting each value into stem and leaf

name: Ogive
definition_quote: Sometimes we sum frequencies and show the result visually in a cumulative relative frequency plot (also known as an ogive).
plain_en: graph of cumulative relative frequencies

name: SOCS
definition_quote: When describing a distribution, always comment on Shape, Outliers, Center, and Spread (SOCS).
plain_en: shape, outliers, center, and spread

name: Symmetric distribution
definition_quote: A symmetric distribution is one in which the two halves are mirror images of each other.
plain_en: distribution with mirror-image halves

name: Skewed right
definition_quote: A distribution is skewed to the right if it spreads far and thinly toward the higher values.
plain_en: distribution with a long right tail

name: Skewed left
definition_quote: A distribution is skewed to the left if it spreads far and thinly toward the lower values.
plain_en: distribution with a long left tail

name: Bell-shaped distribution
definition_quote: A bell-shaped distribution is symmetric with a center mound and two sloping tails.
plain_en: symmetric distribution with a central mound

name: Uniform distribution
definition_quote: A distribution is uniform if its histogram is a horizontal line.
plain_en: distribution with equally likely values

name: Unimodal
definition_quote: A distribution with one main peak is called unimodal and with two distinct peaks is called bimodal.
plain_en: distribution with one main peak

name: Bimodal
definition_quote: A distribution with one main peak is called unimodal and with two distinct peaks is called bimodal.
plain_en: distribution with two distinct peaks

name: Outliers
definition_quote: Outliers are values that are unusually small or large relative to the rest of the data.
plain_en: values far from the rest of the data

name: Gaps
definition_quote: Gaps show holes where no values fall.
plain_en: intervals with no data values

name: Clusters
definition_quote: Clusters show natural subgroups into which the values fall.
plain_en: natural subgroups of data values

name: Center
definition_quote: The center either separates the values (or the area under the curve in a histogram) roughly in half (the median) or is calculated as an average (the mean).
plain_en: typical middle value of a distribution

name: Spread
definition_quote: The spread or variability is the scope of the values from smallest to largest.
plain_en: range of values from smallest to largest

name: Median
definition_quote: The median, which is the middle number of a set of numbers arranged in numerical order.
plain_en: middle value when data are ordered

name: Mean
definition_quote: The mean, which is found by summing items in a set and dividing by the number of items.
plain_en: sum of values divided by count

name: Resistant measure
definition_quote: The median and IQR are called resistant or robust measures because outliers do not greatly (if at all) affect their values.
plain_en: measure not greatly affected by outliers

name: Nonresistant measure
definition_quote: The mean, range, variance, and standard deviation are called nonresistant or nonrobust measures because outliers can greatly affect their values.
plain_en: measure strongly affected by outliers

name: Five-number summary
definition_quote: To understand variability, we either calculate the mean and standard deviation (defined below) or calculate the following five-number summary of a data set:
plain_en: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum

name: First quartile (Q1)
definition_quote: The 25th percentile, Q1, is the median of the lower half of the data set.
plain_en: median of the lower half of data

name: Third quartile (Q3)
definition_quote: The 75th percentile, Q3, is the median of the upper half of the data set.
plain_en: median of the upper half of data

name: Range
definition_quote: Range: the difference between the largest and smallest values (maximum minus minimum).
plain_en: maximum value minus minimum value

name: Interquartile range (IQR)
definition_quote: Interquartile range (IQR): the difference between the largest and smallest values after removing the lower and upper quartiles.
plain_en: spread of the middle half of data

name: Variance
definition_quote: Variance: the average of the squared differences from the mean.
plain_en: average squared distance from the mean

name: Standard deviation
definition_quote: Standard deviation (SD): the square root of the variance.
plain_en: typical distance of values from the mean

name: 1.5 × IQR rule
definition_quote: The more common rule is that outliers are any value less than Q1 - 1.5(IQR) or greater than Q3 + 1.5(IQR).
plain_en: rule flagging values beyond 1.5 IQR

name: Simple ranking
definition_quote: Simple ranking, which involves arranging the elements in some order and noting where in that order a particular value falls.
plain_en: position of a value in an ordered list

name: Percentile ranking
definition_quote: Percentile ranking, which indicates what percentage of all values fall at or below the value under consideration.
plain_en: percent of values at or below a value

name: z-score
definition_quote: The z-score, which states very specifically the number of standard deviations a particular value is above or below the mean.
plain_en: number of standard deviations from the mean

name: Quartiles
definition_quote: Quartiles split data into four equal parts.
plain_en: values dividing data into four parts

name: Deciles
definition_quote: Deciles split data into 10 equal parts.
plain_en: values dividing data into ten parts

name: Boxplot
definition_quote: A boxplot (also called a box and whisker display) is a visual representation displaying the distribution of data that shows the smallest value, the largest value, the middle (median), the middle of the bottom half of the set (Q1), and the middle of the top half of the set (Q3).
plain_en: display showing five-number summary and outliers

name: Comparing distributions
definition_quote: When asked for a comparison, don't forget to address Shape, Unusual features (Outliers, gaps, clusters), Center, and Spread (SOCS or CUSS) and to refer to context.
plain_en: describe shape, outliers, center, and spread comparatively

name: Investigative question
definition_quote: There are three principal components to the investigative question:
plain_en: question a study is designed to answer

name: Random sample
definition_quote: A sample is considered random when all observational units in the sample are selected from the population using some type of random mechanism.
plain_en: sample selected using chance

name: Randomization in sampling
definition_quote: The use of randomization in sample selection increases the chance that the resulting sample exhibits all the known and unknown features of the population.
plain_en: using chance to select a sample

name: Generalizability
definition_quote: A sample is generalizable only to the population from which the sample was selected.
plain_en: applying sample results only to its population

name: Observational study
definition_quote: In an observational study, we simply observe and measure something that has taken place or is taking place while trying not to cause any changes by our presence.
plain_en: study observing without imposing a treatment

name: Experiment
definition_quote: In an experiment, we impose some change or treatment and measure the response.
plain_en: study imposing a treatment and measuring response

name: Cause-and-effect conclusion
definition_quote: It is not possible to conclude a cause-and-effect relationship between variables using data collected from an observational study.
plain_en: concluding one variable causes another

name: Blocking
definition_quote: If there is an important difference among the subjects, similar subjects should be grouped into blocks, and treatments should be randomized within the blocks.
plain_en: grouping similar subjects before random treatment

name: Observational studies
definition_quote: Observational studies aim to gather information about a population without disturbing the population.
plain_en: studies observing a population undisturbed

name: Retrospective study
definition_quote: Retrospective studies look backward, examining existing data, while prospective studies watch for outcomes, tracking individuals into the future.
plain_en: study examining existing past data

name: Prospective study
definition_quote: Retrospective studies look backward, examining existing data, while prospective studies watch for outcomes, tracking individuals into the future.
plain_en: study tracking individuals into the future

name: Sampling variability
definition_quote: Different samples give different statistics, all of which are estimates for the same population parameter.
plain_en: statistics varying from sample to sample

name: Census
definition_quote: Collecting data from every individual in a population, called a census, might seem to provide complete information, but unless the population is small, this method would be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming.
plain_en: attempt to measure an entire population

name: Sampling frame
definition_quote: The list of all individuals from which the sample is drawn is called the sampling frame.
plain_en: list from which a sample is drawn

name: Simple random sample (SRS)
definition_quote: A simple random sample (SRS) is one in which every possible sample of the desired size has an equal chance of being selected.
plain_en: sample where every sample size n is equally likely

name: Stratified random sampling
definition_quote: Stratified random sampling involves dividing the population into non-overlapping homogeneous groups called strata, then picking random samples from each of the strata, and finally combining these individual samples into what is called a stratified random sample.
plain_en: random samples from homogeneous subgroups

name: Strata
definition_quote: Stratified random sampling involves dividing the population into non-overlapping homogeneous groups called strata, then picking random samples from each of the strata, and finally combining these individual samples into what is called a stratified random sample.
plain_en: homogeneous subgroups of a population

name: Proportional sampling
definition_quote: We could further do proportional sampling, where the sizes of the random samples from each stratum depend on the proportion of the total population represented by the stratum.
plain_en: stratum sample sizes matched to population proportions

name: Cluster random sampling
definition_quote: Cluster random sampling involves dividing the population into non-overlapping heterogeneous groups called clusters, each similar to each other, and then picking everyone or everything in a random selection of one or more of the clusters.
plain_en: sample whole randomly chosen heterogeneous groups

name: Systematic random sampling
definition_quote: Systematic random sampling is a relatively simple and quick method. It involves listing the population in some order (for example, alphabetically), choosing a random point to start, and then picking every tenth (or hundredth, or thousandth, or kth) person from the list.
plain_en: choose random start then every kth unit

name: Sampling for homogeneity
definition_quote: However, sometimes we instead randomly pick a sample from each of two or more populations and then compare the distribution of some variable among the different populations. This second method is called sampling for homogeneity.
plain_en: random samples from several populations compared

name: Sampling bias
definition_quote: A sampling method is biased if in some critical way it consistently results in samples that do not represent the population.
plain_en: method consistently producing unrepresentative samples

name: Voluntary response survey
definition_quote: Voluntary response surveys are based on individuals who choose to participate
plain_en: survey of people who choose to respond

name: Convenience survey
definition_quote: Convenience surveys are based on choosing individuals who are easy to reach
plain_en: survey using easily reached individuals

name: Undercoverage bias
definition_quote: Undercoverage bias happens when there is inadequate representation, and thus some groups in the population are left out of the process of choosing the sample.
plain_en: some population groups left out of sampling

name: Response bias
definition_quote: Response bias occurs when the question itself can lead to misleading results because people don't want to be perceived as having unpopular or unsavory views or don't want to admit to having committed crimes.
plain_en: question wording leads to misleading answers

name: Nonresponse bias
definition_quote: Nonresponse bias, where there are low response rates, occurs when individuals chosen for the sample can't be contacted or refuse to participate, and it is often unclear which part of the population is responding.
plain_en: bias from people refusing to respond

name: Experimental unit
definition_quote: An experiment is performed on objects called experimental units.
plain_en: object on which an experiment is performed

name: Subject
definition_quote: If the units are people, they are called subjects.
plain_en: person participating in an experiment

name: Factor
definition_quote: Experiments involve explanatory variables, called factors, that are believed to have an effect on response variables.
plain_en: explanatory variable in an experiment

name: Response variable
definition_quote: A group is intentionally treated with some level of the explanatory variable, and the outcome of the response variable is measured.
plain_en: outcome measured in an experiment

name: Comparison
definition_quote: In comparison, we wish to compare a response variable with regard to two or more experimental conditions (treatments)
plain_en: comparing responses across treatments

name: Control group
definition_quote: If the purpose of an experiment is to determine whether some treatment has an effect, we compare to a control group that doesn't receive that treatment.
plain_en: group not receiving the treatment

name: Placebo
definition_quote: Depending on the experiment, a control group may be given an inactive treatment (a placebo), an established active treatment, or no treatment at all.
plain_en: inactive dummy treatment

name: Blinding
definition_quote: Blinding occurs when the subjects don't know which of the different treatments (such as placebos) they are receiving.
plain_en: subjects unaware of treatment received

name: Double-blinding
definition_quote: Double-blinding is when neither the subjects nor the response evaluators know who is receiving which treatment.
plain_en: subjects and evaluators unaware of treatments

name: Random assignment
definition_quote: In random assignment, we use chance to randomly assign treatments to experimental units:
plain_en: using chance to assign treatments

name: Replication
definition_quote: In replication, the larger the sample is, the more significant the observation:
plain_en: using enough subjects in each treatment

name: Control
definition_quote: Control allows us to minimize the sources of variation other than the treatments by making conditions as similar as possible for all treatment groups:
plain_en: keeping conditions similar across groups

name: Confounding
definition_quote: Two variables are confounded when both are associated with a response variable and are also associated with each other.
plain_en: two variables effects cannot be separated

name: Completely randomized design
definition_quote: Random assignment to treatments, called completely randomized design, is critical in good experimental design.
plain_en: all subjects randomly assigned to treatments

name: Matched pairs design
definition_quote: A matched pairs design (also called a paired comparison design) is when two treatments are compared based on the responses of paired subjects, one of whom receives one treatment while the other receives the second treatment.
plain_en: treatments compared using paired subjects
covers_concepts: Matched pairs design; Paired comparison design

name: Block design
definition_quote: blocking, in experimental design, first divides the subjects into representative groups called blocks based on similar characteristics. Subjects within each block are randomly assigned treatments.
plain_en: randomize treatments within similar blocks

name: Statistically significant
definition_quote: something is statistically significant if the probability of it happening just by chance is so small that you're convinced there must be another explanation.
plain_en: result unlikely to occur by chance alone

name: Bias
definition_quote: Bias: when a study systematically favors certain outcomes
plain_en: study systematically favors certain outcomes

name: Block design (glossary)
definition_quote: Block design: an experimental design where subjects are divided into representative groups to bring certain differences into the picture and reduce variation (for example, blocking by gender, age, or race) and randomization then takes place within each block
plain_en: divide subjects into groups then randomize

name: Explanatory variable
definition_quote: Experiments involve explanatory variables, called factors, that are believed to have an effect on response variables.
plain_en: variable thought to affect the response

name: Two-way table
definition_quote: These data can be displayed in a two-way table (also called a contingency table).
plain_en: table cross-tabulating two categorical variables

name: Marginal frequencies
definition_quote: The row sums and column sums above are called marginal frequencies.
plain_en: row and column totals in a two-way table

name: Marginal relative frequencies
definition_quote: The row sums and column sums above are called marginal relative frequencies.
plain_en: row and column proportions in a two-way table

name: Conditional relative frequencies
definition_quote: Conditional relative frequencies are the relative frequencies for a specific part of the table, for example, the cell frequencies in a row divided by the total for that row or the cell frequencies in a column divided by the total for that column.
plain_en: proportions within one row or column

name: Segmented bar chart
definition_quote: Segmented bar charts are like pie charts, except that the data set is represented by a rectangular bar rather than a circle.
plain_en: bar divided into proportional category segments

name: Association
definition_quote: Because the distributions of focus levels are different for each picture viewed, we say that the two variables, focus level and pictures viewed, are associated.
plain_en: two variables are related

name: Mosaic plot
definition_quote: Mosaic plots are another graphical display that show the cell frequencies in a two-way table.
plain_en: area-based display of two-way table frequencies

name: Simpson’s paradox
definition_quote: This problem is an example of Simpson's paradox, where a conjecture can be reversed when several different groups of data are combined to form a single group.
plain_en: association reverses when groups are combined

name: Probability
definition_quote: Even though we may not be able to foretell a specific result, we can sometimes assign what is called a probability to indicate the likelihood that a particular event will occur.
plain_en: likelihood that an event occurs

name: Event
definition_quote: An event is a collection of one or more outcomes.
plain_en: set of one or more outcomes

name: Relative frequency (probability)
definition_quote: The relative frequency of an event is the proportion of times the event happened-that is, the number of times the event happened divided by the total number of trials.
plain_en: proportion of trials in which event occurs

name: Law of large numbers
definition_quote: The law of large numbers states that when an experiment is performed a large number of times, the relative frequency of an event tends to become closer to the true probability of the event; that is, probability is long-run relative frequency.
plain_en: long-run relative frequency approaches true probability

name: Gambler’s fallacy
definition_quote: The idea that a few outcomes will immediately be balanced by other outcomes is also called the gambler's fallacy.
plain_en: belief that past outcomes must balance soon

name: Complement
definition_quote: The probability that an event will not occur, that is, the probability of its complement, is equal to 1 minus the probability that the event will occur.
plain_en: event not occurring

name: General addition rule
definition_quote: The general addition rule: P(A or B or both) = P(A union B) = P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B).
plain_en: probability of either event minus overlap

name: Mutually exclusive
definition_quote: A and B are mutually exclusive if A ∩ B = ∅ or, equivalently, P(A ∩ B) = 0.
plain_en: events that cannot occur together

name: General multiplication rule
definition_quote: The general multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A intersect B) = P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B|A).
plain_en: probability of both events using conditional probability

name: Independent events
definition_quote: A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A) or, equivalently, P(B|A) = P(B).
plain_en: one event does not change the other's probability

name: Conditional probability
definition_quote: Conditional probabilities shrink the population of interest.
plain_en: probability given that another event occurred

name: Random variable
definition_quote: If X represents the different numbers associated with the potential outcomes of some chance situation, we call X a random variable.
plain_en: numerical outcome of a chance process

name: Expected value
definition_quote: The expected value or mean of a discrete random variable X is given by μ X = E(X) = ∑ xP(x), where P(x) is the probability of outcome x.
plain_en: probability-weighted average outcome
covers_concepts: Expected value; Mean of a random variable

name: Weighted average
definition_quote: The expected value is sometimes referred to as a weighted average.
plain_en: average weighted by probabilities

name: Variance of a discrete random variable
name_normalized: variance of a discrete random variable
definition_quote: If we regard the (x - μ)2 terms as the values of some discrete random variable (whose probability is the same as the probability of x), the mean of this new discrete random variable is ∑(xi - μx)2pi, which is precisely how we define the variance, σ2, of a discrete random variable:
plain_en: probability-weighted average squared deviation

name: Adding variances of independent random variables
name_normalized: adding variances of independent random variables
definition_quote: Variances of independent random variables can be added together, but standard deviations cannot!
plain_en: independent variances add but standard deviations do not

name: Probability distribution
definition_quote: A probability distribution is a list or formula that gives the probability of each outcome.
plain_en: list or formula of outcome probabilities

name: Binomial setting
definition_quote: We have a binomial setting when the following conditions are met: ■There are two possible outcomes, often referred to as success and failure. ■There are a fixed number of trials, n. ■The trials are independent; that is, the outcome of one trial does not affect the outcome of any other trial.
plain_en: fixed independent trials with two outcomes

name: Binomial random variable
definition_quote: The binomial probability function refers to a binomial random variable X with n independent trials and probability of success p.
plain_en: count of successes in binomial trials

name: binompdf
definition_quote: binompdf (n, p, x) gives the probability of exactly x successes in n trials, where p is the probability of success on a single trial.
plain_en: calculator probability of exactly x successes

name: binomcdf
definition_quote: binomcdf (n, p, x) gives the cumulative probability of x or fewer successes in n trials, where p is the probability of success on a single trial.
plain_en: calculator probability of at most x successes

name: Mean of a binomial distribution
definition_quote: The expected value or mean number of successes is np.
plain_en: expected successes equals n times p

name: Shape of a binomial distribution
definition_quote: The shape of a binomial distribution is skewed right when p < 0.5, symmetric when p = 0.5, and skewed left when p > 0.5.
plain_en: binomial shape depends on success probability

name: Probability distribution (function)
definition_quote: A probability distribution is a function, table, or graph that links outcomes of a statistical experiment with its probability of occurrence.
plain_en: function linking outcomes to probabilities

name: Cumulative probability distribution
definition_quote: A cumulative probability distribution is a function, table, or graph that links outcomes with the probability of less than or equal to that outcome occurring.
plain_en: probability of at most a given outcome

name: Normal distribution
definition_quote: One bell-shaped distribution, called the normal distribution, is valuable for providing a useful model in describing various natural phenomena.
plain_en: bell-shaped symmetric probability model

name: Points of inflection
definition_quote: There is a point on each side where the slope is steepest. These two points are called points of inflection, and the distance from the mean to either point is precisely equal to one standard deviation.
plain_en: curve points one standard deviation from mean

name: Normal parameters
definition_quote: Every normal distribution is completely determined by two parameters: its mean μ and its standard deviation s.
plain_en: mean and standard deviation define a normal curve

name: Empirical rule
definition_quote: The empirical rule (also called the 68-95-99.7 rule) applies specifically to normal distributions. About 68% of the values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% of the values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, and about 99.7% of the values lie within 3 standard deviations of the mean.
plain_en: 68, 95, and 99.7 percent within 1, 2, 3 SDs

name: Standard normal distribution
definition_quote: normalcdf(lowerbd, upperbd) = probability between two z-scores for the standard normal distribution (mean = 0 and SD = 1)
plain_en: normal distribution with mean zero and SD one

name: normalcdf
definition_quote: normalcdf(lowerbd, upperbd, mean, SD) = probability between two raw scores for a normal distribution with the given mean and SD
plain_en: calculator normal probability between two values

name: invNorm
definition_quote: invNorm(probability) = z-score with the given probability to the left for the standard normal distribution (mean = 0 and SD = 1)
plain_en: calculator value with given left probability

name: Normal approximation to the binomial
definition_quote: A general rule of thumb is that the normal is a good approximation to the binomial whenever both np and n(1 - p) are at least 10.
plain_en: use normal when np and n(1-p) are large

name: Sampling distribution
definition_quote: The probability distribution showing how a statistic varies is called a sampling distribution.
plain_en: distribution of a statistic over samples

name: Central limit theorem
definition_quote: The following principle, called the central limit theorem of statistics (abbreviated CLT), forms the basis of much of what we discuss in this and the following units. Start with a population with any shape distribution whatsoever. Pick n sufficiently large (at least 30), and take all samples of size n. Compute the mean of each of these samples. Then the set of all sample means is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: sample means become normal for large samples

name: Mean of the sampling distribution of x̅
name_normalized: mean of the sampling distribution of x̅
definition_quote: the mean μ x̅ of the sampling distribution of x̅ equals the population mean μ.
plain_en: sample mean averages to population mean

name: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̅
name_normalized: standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̅
definition_quote: the standard deviation σ x̅ of the sampling distribution of x̅ equals the population standard deviation σ divided by the square root of the sample size.
plain_en: population SD divided by square root n

name: Randomization distribution
definition_quote: One example of a sampling distribution is a randomization distribution, a collection of statistics generated by simulation.
plain_en: simulated distribution created by random reassignment

name: Binomial distribution
definition_quote: The binomial probability function refers to a binomial random variable X with n independent trials and probability of success p.
plain_en: distribution of successes in fixed independent trials

name: Bias in a sampling distribution
definition_quote: In the context of sampling distributions, bias means that the sampling distribution of an estimator is not centered on the population parameter.
plain_en: estimator distribution not centered on parameter

name: Unbiased estimator
definition_quote: An estimator is unbiased if, on average, it does not underestimate or overestimate the population parameter.
plain_en: estimator averages to the population parameter

name: Point estimator
definition_quote: Sample statistics are point estimators for population parameters.
plain_en: sample statistic used to estimate a parameter

name: Sampling distribution of a sample proportion
name_normalized: sampling distribution of a sample proportion
definition_quote: The set of all sample proportions is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: distribution of sample proportions from repeated samples

name: Mean of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
name_normalized: mean of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
definition_quote: The mean of the set of sample proportions equals p, the population proportion.
plain_en: sample proportion averages to population proportion

name: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
name_normalized: standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
definition_quote: The standard deviation of the set of sample proportions is approximately equal to
plain_en: spread of sample proportions decreases with n

name: Randomization condition
definition_quote: The randomization condition: The data should be collected using a random sample.
plain_en: data come from a random sample

name: 10% condition
definition_quote: The 10% condition: When sampling without replacement, the sample size n should be no larger than 10% of the population.
plain_en: sample no more than ten percent of population

name: Normality condition for proportions
definition_quote: The normality condition: The number of successes, np, and the number of failures, n(1 - p), should both be at least 10.
plain_en: at least ten successes and ten failures

name: Confidence interval
definition_quote: First, there is the confidence interval. This gives an interval of plausible values and is expressed in the following form: estimate ± margin of error
plain_en: range of plausible parameter values

name: Confidence level
definition_quote: Second, there is the success rate for the method, called the confidence level. This is the proportion of times repeated applications of this method would capture the true population parameter.
plain_en: long-run success rate of the method

name: Critical value z*
definition_quote: where the critical value, z*, depends on the chosen confidence level.
plain_en: multiplier set by the confidence level

name: One-sample z-interval for a population proportion
name_normalized: one-sample z-interval for a population proportion
definition_quote: Naming the procedure is most easily done by simply stating "one-sample z-interval for a population proportion."
plain_en: confidence interval for one proportion

name: Interpreting a confidence level
definition_quote: Second, we can interpret the confidence level and say that if this survey were conducted many times, about 90% of the resulting confidence intervals would contain the true proportion of voters who favor the bond issue.
plain_en: percent of intervals capturing the parameter

name: Choosing sample size for a proportion
name_normalized: choosing sample size for a proportion
definition_quote: A formula for choosing the sample size n for a specific margin of error, MOE, can be found by algebraically solving for n in the equation to obtain:
plain_en: sample size needed for a margin of error

name: Null hypothesis
definition_quote: The general testing procedure is to choose a specific hypothesis to be tested, called the null hypothesis, pick an appropriate random sample, and then use measurements from the sample to determine the likelihood of the null hypothesis.
plain_en: hypothesis of no effect or no difference

name: Alternative hypothesis
definition_quote: There is an alternative hypothesis, stated in the form of a strict inequality (for example, Ha: p < 0.37 or Ha: p > 0.37 or Ha: p ≠ 0.37).
plain_en: hypothesis the test hopes to support

name: p-value
definition_quote: The strength of the sample statistic can be gauged through its associated p-value, which is the probability of obtaining a sample statistic as extreme (or more extreme) as the one obtained if the null hypothesis is assumed to be true.
plain_en: probability of results as extreme under null

name: Significance level
definition_quote: The significance level, α, is fixed at the beginning of the hypothesis test.
plain_en: threshold fixed before the test

name: Type I error
definition_quote: The α-risk, also called the significance level of the test, is the probability of committing a Type I error and mistakenly rejecting a true null hypothesis.
plain_en: rejecting a true null hypothesis

name: Type II error
definition_quote: A Type II error, a mistaken failure to reject a false null hypothesis, has associated probability β.
plain_en: failing to reject a false null hypothesis

name: Power
definition_quote: The power of a hypothesis test is the probability that a Type II error is not committed. That is, given a true alternative, the power is the probability of rejecting the false null hypothesis.
plain_en: probability of rejecting a false null

name: One-sided test
definition_quote: For a one-sided test (the alternative is < or >), the p-value is the proportion of values at or more extreme than the test statistic (in the direction of the alternative).
plain_en: test with a directional alternative

name: Two-sided test
definition_quote: For a two-sided test (the alternative is ≠), the p-value is the proportion of values at or more extreme than the test statistic in either direction; that is, it is twice the calculated tail probability.
plain_en: test with a not-equal alternative

name: Decision rule for a hypothesis test
name_normalized: decision rule for a hypothesis test
definition_quote: If the p-value ≤α, reject H0; there is convincing evidence for Ha. If the p-value >α, fail to reject H0; there is not convincing evidence for Ha.
plain_en: compare p-value with significance level

name: One-sample z-test for a population proportion
name_normalized: one-sample z-test for a population proportion
definition_quote: Procedure: One-sample z-test for a population proportion.
plain_en: hypothesis test for one proportion

name: Sampling distribution of the difference in sample proportions
name_normalized: sampling distribution of the difference in sample proportions
definition_quote: The set of all differences of sample proportions is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: distribution of differences between sample proportions

name: Mean of the difference in sample proportions
name_normalized: mean of the difference in sample proportions
definition_quote: The mean of the set of differences of sample proportions equals p1 - p2, the difference of population proportions.
plain_en: difference averages to population difference

name: Standard deviation of the difference in sample proportions
name_normalized: standard deviation of the difference in sample proportions
definition_quote: The standard deviation of the set of differences of sample proportions is approximately equal to
plain_en: spread of difference between sample proportions

name: Randomization condition for two samples
definition_quote: The randomization condition: The data should be collected using random samples, and the samples must be taken independently of each other.
plain_en: independent random samples required

name: Normality condition for two proportions
definition_quote: The normality condition: The numbers of successes, n1 p1 and n2 p2, and the numbers of failures, n1(1 - p1) and n2(1 - p2), should all be at least 10.
plain_en: at least ten successes and failures per group

name: Two-sample z-interval for a difference in proportions
name_normalized: two-sample z-interval for a difference in proportions
definition_quote: A confidence interval for the difference of two proportions will take the following form:
plain_en: interval estimate for difference of proportions

name: Null hypothesis for a difference of two proportions
name_normalized: null hypothesis for a difference of two proportions
definition_quote: The null hypothesis for a difference of two proportions is H0 : p1 = p2.
plain_en: hypothesis that two proportions are equal

name: Alternative hypothesis for a difference of two proportions
name_normalized: alternative hypothesis for a difference of two proportions
definition_quote: The alternative hypothesis is Ha : p1 > p2, Ha : p1 < p2, or Ha : p1 ≠ p2.
plain_en: hypothesis that proportions differ

name: Pooled proportion
definition_quote: With a null hypothesis of H0 : p1 = p2, we use the combined (or pooled) proportion in the normality condition and in calculating the standard error.
plain_en: combined proportion used under equal proportions

name: Two-sample z-test for a difference in proportions
name_normalized: two-sample z-test for a difference in proportions
definition_quote: Procedure: Two-sample z-test for a difference of two population proportions.
plain_en: hypothesis test comparing two proportions

name: Chi-square test for independence
definition_quote: We cross-classify a single sample of observations from a single population in two ways and then ask whether the two variables are independent of each other. This leads to chi-square tests for independence with hypotheses:
plain_en: test association between two categorical variables

name: Chi-square test for homogeneity
definition_quote: There is a related class of problems in which we have a single categorical variable and obtain independent samples from two or more populations to determine whether the distributions of that variable are different for the populations. This leads to chi-square tests for homogeneity with hypotheses:
plain_en: test whether distributions differ across populations

name: Expected values condition
definition_quote: The expected values condition: All expected values should be greater than 5.
plain_en: all expected cell counts exceed five

name: Expected values
definition_quote: Expected values are calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true.
plain_en: cell counts expected under the null

name: Chi-square statistic
definition_quote: The significance of the differences is gauged by a χ2-value of weighted squared differences defined by:
plain_en: weighted sum of squared differences

name: Degrees of freedom for a chi-square test
name_normalized: degrees of freedom for a chi-square test
definition_quote: df = (rows - 1)(columns - 1)
plain_en: rows minus one times columns minus one

name: Chi-square distribution
definition_quote: the χ2-distribution is a continuous distribution. Applying it to counting data is just an approximation.
plain_en: continuous approximation for count data

name: Margin of error
definition_quote: The percent is the percent of samples that would pinpoint the unknown p within plus or minus respective margins of error.
plain_en: half-width of a confidence interval

name: Sampling distribution of the sample mean
name_normalized: sampling distribution of the sample mean
definition_quote: If the population is approximately normal, or if the sample size is large enough (at least 30) for the central limit theorem to apply, we also have that the set of sample means is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: distribution of sample means over repeated samples

name: Mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean
name_normalized: mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean
definition_quote: The mean of the set of sample means equals
plain_en: sample means average to population mean

name: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean
name_normalized: standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean
definition_quote: The standard deviation of the set of sample means is approximately equal to
plain_en: population SD divided by square root n

name: Normality condition for means
definition_quote: The normality condition: Either the population distribution should be approximately normal or the sample size n should be ≥ 30, or if n < 30, the sample data should be free from strong skewness and outliers.
plain_en: normal population or large sample or symmetric data

name: t-distribution
definition_quote: with a resulting t-distribution that is bell-shaped and symmetric but lower at the mean, higher at the tails, and so more spread out than the normal distribution.
plain_en: bell-shaped distribution with heavier tails

name: Degrees of freedom
definition_quote: In the tables, these distinct t-distributions are associated with the values for degrees of freedom (df). For this discussion, the df value is equal to the sample size minus 1.
plain_en: sample size minus one for one-sample t

name: When to use the t-distribution
definition_quote: Thus, the t-distribution is the proper choice whenever the population standard deviation σ is unknown.
plain_en: use t when population SD is unknown

name: Critical value t*
definition_quote: where the critical value, t*, depends on the chosen confidence level and on the degrees of freedom, df = n - 1.
plain_en: t multiplier for confidence level and df

name: One-sample t-interval for a population mean
name_normalized: one-sample t-interval for a population mean
definition_quote: Naming the procedure is easiest done by simply stating "one-sample t-interval for a population mean."
plain_en: confidence interval for one mean

name: One-sample t-interval for a population mean difference
name_normalized: one-sample t-interval for a population mean difference
definition_quote: For this matched pairs design, the procedure is called a "one-sample t-interval for a population mean difference."
plain_en: interval for mean of paired differences

name: One-sample t-test for a population mean
name_normalized: one-sample t-test for a population mean
definition_quote: Procedure: A one-sample t-test for a population mean (population SD is unknown)
plain_en: hypothesis test for one mean

name: One-sample t-test for a population mean difference
name_normalized: one-sample t-test for a population mean difference
definition_quote: Procedure: A one-sample t-test for a population mean difference (the mean difference of reaction times, before minus after)
plain_en: hypothesis test for paired differences

name: Mean of the difference in sample means
name_normalized: mean of the difference in sample means
definition_quote: The mean of the set of differences of sample means equals the difference of population means.
plain_en: difference averages to population difference

name: Standard deviation of the difference in sample means
name_normalized: standard deviation of the difference in sample means
definition_quote: The standard deviation of the set of differences of sample means is approximately equal to
plain_en: spread of difference between sample means

name: Normality of the difference in sample means
name_normalized: normality of the difference in sample means
definition_quote: If the populations are normal or if the sample sizes are large enough (at least 30) for the central limit theorem to apply, we also have that the set of all differences of sample means is approximately normally distributed.
plain_en: difference of means is approximately normal

name: Two-sample t-interval for a difference of means
name_normalized: two-sample t-interval for a difference of means
definition_quote: The confidence interval takes the following form:
plain_en: interval estimate for difference of two means

name: Null hypothesis for two means
definition_quote: The null hypothesis is usually that the means of the populations are the same or, equivalently, that their difference is 0:
plain_en: hypothesis that two population means are equal

name: Alternative hypothesis for two means
definition_quote: The alternative hypothesis is then:
plain_en: hypothesis that the two means differ

name: Two-sample t-test for a difference of means
name_normalized: two-sample t-test for a difference of means
definition_quote: Procedure: A two-sample t-test for the difference of two population means
plain_en: hypothesis test comparing two means

name: No pooling in a two-sample t-test
name_normalized: no pooling in a two-sample t-test
definition_quote: You should not pool in a two-sample t-test like we did in a two- proportion z- test.
plain_en: do not pool standard deviations for two means

name: Simulation p-value
definition_quote: We can use a simulation to determine what values of a test statistic are likely to occur by random chance alone, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Then looking at where our test statistic falls, we can estimate a p-value.
plain_en: estimate p-value from simulated statistics

name: Power given a specific alternative
definition_quote: Given a specific alternative hypothesis, a Type II error is a mistaken failure to reject the false null hypothesis, while the power is the probability of rejecting that false null hypothesis.
plain_en: probability of rejecting a false null

name: Factors that increase power
definition_quote: A general conclusion is that if the other three values below are unchanged, the power will increase (and the probability of a Type II error will decrease) if any of the following occur:
plain_en: power rises with alpha, n, effect, lower SE

name: Effect size
definition_quote: The difference between p0 and p is sometimes called the effect-thus the greater the effect, the greater is the power.
plain_en: distance between null and true parameter

name: Choosing a confidence interval
definition_quote: An estimate of an unknown population parameter indicates a confidence interval.
plain_en: estimate requested means use interval

name: Choosing a hypothesis test
definition_quote: A claim about a population parameter indicates a hypothesis test.
plain_en: claim requested means use hypothesis test

name: Confidence interval and hypothesis test consistency
name_normalized: confidence interval and hypothesis test consistency
definition_quote: If a 95% confidence interval for μ captures μ0, there is not sufficient evidence to reject H0 : μ = μ0 in a two-sided test with α = 0.05.
plain_en: interval containing null value matches non-rejection

name: Standard error
definition_quote: In this case is called the standard error, , and is used as an estimate for
plain_en: estimated standard deviation of a statistic

name: Correlation coefficient
definition_quote: A numerical measurement, r, which is called the correlation coefficient (or simply the correlation), gives a quantitative value of the strength of a linear relationship.
plain_en: number measuring strength of linear association

name: Scatterplot
definition_quote: A scatterplot gives an immediate visual impression of the strength of a linear relationship.
plain_en: graph of two quantitative variables

name: Positively associated
definition_quote: When larger values of one variable are associated with larger values of a second variable, the variables are called positively associated.
plain_en: both variables increase together

name: Negatively associated
definition_quote: When larger values of one variable are associated with smaller values of a second variable, the variables are called negatively associated.
plain_en: one variable increases as the other decreases

name: Coefficient of determination
definition_quote: The coefficient of determination, r2, is the proportion of variation in the observed values that is explained by the linear model.
plain_en: proportion of variation explained by the line

name: Labeled scatterplot
definition_quote: Sometimes different dots in a scatterplot are labeled with different symbols or different colors to show a categorical variable.
plain_en: scatterplot marking a categorical group

name: DUFS
definition_quote: DUFS + context (Direction, Unusual features, Form, and Strength)
plain_en: direction, unusual features, form, strength

name: Correlation
definition_quote: there is a mathematical measure called correlation coefficient (or simply the correlation). Correlation measures strength and gives the direction of a linear relationship.
plain_en: measure of strength and direction of linear association

name: Range of the correlation coefficient
definition_quote: The value of r always falls between -1 and +1.
plain_en: correlation is between minus one and one

name: Coefficient of determination (response variable)
definition_quote: The coefficient of determination, r2, is the proportion of variation in the response variable y that is explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable x.
plain_en: variation in y explained by x

name: Correlation does not imply causation
definition_quote: Correlation does not imply causation!
plain_en: association does not prove a cause

name: Least squares regression line
definition_quote: This best-fitting straight line-that is, the line that minimizes the sum of the squares of the differences between the observed values and the values predicted by the line-is called the least squares regression line, or simply the regression line.
plain_en: line minimizing squared vertical prediction errors
covers_concepts: Least squares regression line; Regression line

name: Predicted value
definition_quote: A variable with a hat (ŷ) is a predicted value of the variable.
plain_en: value estimated by the regression model

name: Slope of the regression line
definition_quote: The slope is the amount that the predicted y-value changes for every unit increase in x.
plain_en: predicted change in y per unit x

name: y-intercept of the regression line
definition_quote: Similarly, the y-intercept is the predicted y-value for x = 0.
plain_en: predicted y when x equals zero

name: Residual
definition_quote: The difference between an observed and a predicted value is called the residual. When the regression line is graphed on the scatterplot, the residual of a point is the vertical distance the point is from the regression line.
plain_en: observed value minus predicted value

name: Residual order
definition_quote: Order is important: residual = y - ŷ = observed y minus predicted y.
plain_en: observed minus predicted, not the reverse

name: Sum of residuals
definition_quote: The sum, and thus the mean, of the residuals is always zero.
plain_en: residuals always sum to zero

name: Residual plot
definition_quote: To obtain a residual plot, the residuals can be plotted against either the x-values or the ŷ-values.
plain_en: graph of residuals against x or predicted y

name: Pattern in a residual plot
definition_quote: A residual plot with a definite pattern is an indication that a nonlinear model will show a better fit to the data than the straight regression line.
plain_en: pattern means a curved model may fit better

name: Standard deviation of the residuals
definition_quote: The standard deviation of the residuals gives a measure of how the points are spread around the regression line.
plain_en: typical distance of points from the line

name: Selecting an inference procedure
definition_quote: Of the six free-response questions on the AP Statistics exam, at least one-and often two-involves inference. For these problems, the first thought should be to identify the appropriate inference method.
plain_en: choose the correct inference method first

name: Choosing a distribution for inference
definition_quote: Which distribution should be used for inference problems? ■Proportions? Use z. ■Means? Use t. ■Counts? Use χ2.
plain_en: z for proportions, t for means, chi-square for counts

name: Choosing a confidence interval or hypothesis test
name_normalized: choosing a confidence interval or hypothesis test
definition_quote: What specifically are you asked to do? ■Estimate a quantity (indicating a confidence interval)? ■Look for evidence to test a claim (indicating a hypothesis test)?
plain_en: estimate means interval, claim means test

name: Describing a one-variable distribution
definition_quote: The distribution of (context) has a shape that is roughly (symmetric/unimodal/bimodal/bell-shaped/skewed left/skewed right/uniform), (center/mean/median) of ____, (range of ____ /IQR of ____ /spread from ____ to ____), and unusual features of (outliers, gaps, clusters).
plain_en: template for shape, center, spread, unusual features

name: Comparing one-variable distributions
definition_quote: The (first distribution in context) has a ____ shape that is (similar/not similar) to the (second distribution in context) that has a ____ shape, the (first distribution in context) has a (larger/smaller/equal) center to the (second distribution in context), the (first distribution in context) has a (larger/smaller/equal) variability to the (second distribution in context), and the (distribution in context) has (outliers/gaps/clusters) although the (distribution in context) (also does/doesn't).
plain_en: template comparing shape, center, variability, unusual features

name: Interpreting the standard deviation
definition_quote: The mean distance between individual (values in context) and the mean (context) is approximately ____.
plain_en: typical distance of values from the mean

name: Interpreting a z-score
definition_quote: The (value in context) is ____ standard deviations (above/below) the mean (value in context).
plain_en: distance from mean in standard deviations

name: Describing a scatterplot
definition_quote: There is a (strong/moderate/weak), (positive/negative), (linear/nonlinear) association between (the explanatory variable x in context) and (the response variable y in context).
plain_en: template for strength, direction, form, context

name: Interpreting the slope
definition_quote: The predicted increase in (response variable y in context) is ___ for each unit increase in (explanatory variable x in context).
plain_en: predicted change in y per one unit x

name: Interpreting the y-intercept
definition_quote: ____ is the predicted value of the (response variable y in context) when the (explanatory variable x in context) is equal to 0.
plain_en: predicted y when x is zero

name: Interpreting R-squared
definition_quote: ____% of the variation in (the y-variable in context) is accounted for by the linear model relating (the y-variable in context) to (the x-variable in context).
plain_en: percent of y variation explained by x

name: Checking conditions for inference
definition_quote: We check (1) the randomization condition (random sample), (2) the 10% condition (if sampling without replacement, the sample is less than the 10% of the population), and (3) the normality condition (for proportions: np≥ 10 and n(1 - p) ≥ 10; and for means: either the population is roughly normal OR the sample size n ≥ 30 OR the sample distribution has no strong skewness or outliers).
plain_en: random, ten percent, and normality conditions

name: Describing a sampling distribution
definition_quote: The sampling distribution for (p̂ / x̅ /b) is approximately normal with mean (p = ____ OR μ = ____ OR β =____ ) and standard deviation
plain_en: template for center and spread of a statistic

name: Interpreting a confidence interval
definition_quote: We are ____ % confident that the true (proportion/mean in context) is between ____ and ____.
plain_en: template stating confidence and interval bounds

name: Interpreting a confidence level
definition_quote: If we take all possible samples of (size in context) and if a confidence interval for the (proportion/mean in context) is constructed from each sample, then ____ % of these intervals will capture the true (proportion/mean in context).
plain_en: percent of intervals capturing the parameter

name: Interpreting a p-value
definition_quote: Assuming that (the null hypothesis in context) is true, there is a probability of ____ of getting a sample (proportion/mean) as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed by chance alone in a random sample of (size in context).
plain_en: probability of extreme result under the null

name: Concluding a test when rejecting the null
name_normalized: concluding a test when rejecting the null
definition_quote: Because the p-value is so small, p = ____ < (significance level), there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. There is convincing evidence that (alternative hypothesis in context).
plain_en: template for rejecting the null hypothesis

name: Concluding a test when failing to reject the null
name_normalized: concluding a test when failing to reject the null
definition_quote: Because the p-value is so large, p = ____ > (significance level), there is not sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. There is not convincing evidence that (alternative hypothesis in context).
plain_en: template for failing to reject the null

name: Interpreting a Type I error
definition_quote: Because the p-value was small, there was sufficient evidence to reject the (null hypothesis in context). However, the null hypothesis might have been true, in which case we committed a Type I error. A possible consequence would be ____.
plain_en: template for rejecting a true null

name: Interpreting a Type II error
definition_quote: Because the p-value was large, there was not sufficient evidence to reject the (null hypothesis in context). However, the null hypothesis might have been false, in which case we committed a Type II error. A possible consequence would be ____.
plain_en: template for failing to reject a false null

name: Interpreting power
definition_quote: There is a (power) probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis.
plain_en: probability of correctly rejecting the null

name: Names of inference procedures
definition_quote: When asked to identify the appropriate inference procedure, the answer should be a complete proper name as in the following expressions.
plain_en: use the complete procedure name
